children: President Donald Trump renewed pressure on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, arguing that the United States should have the cheapest borrowing costs in the world regardless of current economic data, Reuters reported Sunday.

Trump made the comments to reporters at the Irish Open golf tournament ahead of the Fed’s Sept. 15-16 policy meeting. The central bank has held its benchmark rate at 3.5% to 3.75%, but persistent inflation has strengthened the case for another increase.

Consumer prices rose 0.4% in August, the biggest monthly gain in four months, while annual inflation reached 3.4%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, increased 0.3% for the month.

The conflict between Trump’s demand for lower rates and the Fed’s inflation concerns creates added uncertainty for stocks, bonds and the dollar. A rate increase could pressure equity valuations and raise borrowing costs, while holding rates steady despite hotter inflation could push longer-term Treasury yields higher if investors question the central bank’s resolve.

Trump has been less critical of the Fed since Kevin Warsh, his choice for chairman, took office earlier this year. Still, the president recently threatened trade restrictions against countries with which the U.S. runs deficits unless rates come down.

Economists remain divided. A recent Reuters poll found that about 70% expected the Fed to leave rates unchanged at the September meeting, although a growing minority anticipated an increase. Reuters reported that expectations had shifted toward tighter policy as economic data remained strong.
